items.title: I turned my house into a VIDEO GAME!
items.author: NetworkChuck
items.transcript: GPT-6 Astra helped me turn my house into a video game. What happens in the game happens in the real world and vice versa. So, I started with the video. I literally just got my phone out and recorded every single room. And then I gave this like 10-minute video to Astra and said, "Hey, make my house." Everyone said it was pretty good at 3D modeling. Everyone was right. It created my house, a 3D world I can walk around. And did it get it right on the first try? No. We chatted back and forth and then I'm like, "Let's add some more features, like multiplayer." Everyone in my family has a character modeled after them. [music] And we can play at the same time. And then I'm like, "Let's add my dogs. Let's have them walk around. Let's play fetch with them." Astra built this entire game. [music] I actually traveled to OpenAI during me building this and I could do this remotely. ChatGPT [music] on my phone actually accessing my Mac Studio where I was building this. Through context compactions and multiple chats, it kept track [music] of what was going on. And it didn't just build it, it tested its own work. It would open things up and inspect them. Computer use and browser [music] use. I hooked Astra up to my home assistant integration. So, now when I walk up to a light in the game and turn it off, the light in the actual house turns off. Same thing goes for the TV. I can control our TV, our Apple TV from the game and I can see what's on the TV in the game. I've never been able [music] to do something like this and I've been trying for a long time with every single model that's come out. This one is different. So, right now you do need to try GPT-6 Astra in the ChatGPT app [music] and see what you can do.

items.title: your house needs TWO networks (here's why)
items.summary:
Try Flare for free: https://ntck.co/flare-opnsense

Your smart fridge could be the way a hacker gets into your home network. So in part two of Mike's network build, I use OPNsense and VLANs to split his one flat network into separate networks for work, users, and a quarantined IoT network that can't touch anything else. The firewall is the mini PC from Japan we built in part one, the switch is a QNAP I'd never used (it has a dent), and DHCP almost broke me over one hidden checkbox. Then I told Mike his IoT devices were finally locked down, and he asked me what an IoT device is.

In this video you'll learn what a VLAN actually is and how to create one in OPNsense, how trunk (tagged) and untagged ports work on a managed switch, how to give each new network its own gateway IP and DHCP range (plus the one DHCP setting Claude Code had to find for me), how deny-by-default firewall rules and an alias keep your IoT devices locked in their own corner, and what happens when you point an AI agent
